{{Short description|German mathematician}}
[[File:Christoph Thiele.jpg|thumb|Thiele at [[Oberwolfach]], 2011]]

'''Christoph Thiele''' (born 10. September 1968 in [[Darmstadt]]) is a German [[mathematician]] working in the field of [[harmonic analysis]]. After completing his undergraduate studies at [[TU Darmstadt]] and [[Bielefeld University]], he obtained his Ph.D. in 1995 at [[Yale]] under the supervision of [[Ronald Coifman]]. After spending time at [[UCLA]], where he was promoted to full professor, he occupied the [[Felix Hausdorff|Hausdorff]] Chair at the [[University of Bonn]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.hcm.uni-bonn.de/de/people/profile/christoph-thiele/|title = HCM: Prof. Dr. Christoph Thiele}}</ref>

He is famous for work (joint with [[Michael Lacey (mathematician)|Michael Lacey]]) on the bilinear [[Hilbert transform]] and for giving a simplified proof of [[Carleson's theorem]]; the techniques in this proof have deeply influenced the field of [[time–frequency analysis]]. He was a recipient of the 1996 [[Salem Prize]],<ref name="Laboratoire de Mathématiques Raphaël Salem k803">{{cite web | title=Prix Salem | website=Laboratoire de Mathématiques Raphaël Salem | url=https://lmrs.univ-rouen.fr/fr/content/prix-salem | language=fr | access-date=15 November 2023}}</ref> an invited speaker at the 2002 [[International Congress of Mathematicians]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.mathunion.org/icm-plenary-and-invited-speakers|title = ICM Plenary and Invited Speakers &#124; International Mathematical Union (IMU)}}</ref> and a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list|title = Fellows of the American Mathematical Society}}</ref>
